column5: Fabe's introduction argues for shot-by-shot analysis as the way to learn film technique. Her 14-director sequence (Griffith to Figgis) gives a set of case studies the course can point to for editing, POV and sound. Her 'closely watched films' title is an allusion to Menzel's film; her own book uses the term as a method.

Griffith's editing grammar as Fabe sets it out: match cut (movement, direction, eyeline), POV then reaction shot, cross-cutting for suspense, and fades or irises to mark time. Fabe's shot-by-shot method shows how the same grammar carries meaning. Good for the course's editing and coverage sections; cite the device, not her paraphrase.

Fabe notes that Griffith's 'Lonely Villa' cross-cutting (father, intruders, mother) became the 'last-minute rescue' convention. Useful as a suspense example; her shot-level analysis is the reason to read it.
Fabe dates Edison's Fred Ott's Sneeze to 1888. It was filmed in 1894 for the Kinetoscope. Check the date before the course cites it as the first close-up.
The 'writing history with lightning' remark attributed to Wilson after the White House screening is widely repeated but its source is disputed. Do not quote it as fact.
The chapter dates Griffith's Intolerance to 1919. It is 1916; the book's own chapter 1 gives 1916. Correct before citing.

Montage as Fabe sets it out: Kuleshov's experiments (same actor's face placed before soup, a coffin, a child) show meaning comes from juxtaposition. Eisenstein used shock and conflict (screen direction, light, tempo, vertical against horizontal). The Odessa Steps sequence builds tension through short shots of falling, fleeing and the pram. Good for the course's editing and pacing module.
The book says the Odessa Steps have 120 steps. The commonly cited count is 192. Check before the course gives a number.

Fabe on time and space in the Odessa Steps: repeated shots and cross-cutting stretch about a minute of action to five minutes. The mother's fall uses ten shots, some of seven or eight seconds. Lion composite from three separate lions. Useful as a case of how time is built in editing, not as fact about the event.

Fabe on angle and lens as expression: high angle diminishes a character, low angle raises him (The Last Laugh's doorman). Subjective distortion through lenses and superimposition, and a moving camera strapped to the operator, carry the character's state of mind. Use for the lens and camera-angle sections, citing the device, not the book's wording.
Forced-perspective city in The Last Laugh (model towers, graded street, toy cars). Good background on how scale was faked in 1924; not a technique the course needs to teach.

Fabe's two-style frame: realist style uses long takes, depth of focus, medium shots and invisible editing; expressionist style uses montage, distorted optics and an 'unchained' camera. She stresses formal realism (how a film is shot) is not the same as realism of content. Useful for the course's choice between long-take and cut-based coverage.

Fabe's point that a 47-second single take in The Adventurer took many retakes, and that editing removes dead time. Chaplin's ice-cream gag used a stop-start camera trick. Use as a reminder that a long take costs more in retakes, not less.

The text dates the Eisenstein, Pudovkin and Alexandrov sound manifesto to 1929. It was published in 1928. Also the His Girl Friday figure credit gives 1939, while the text says 1940 (the release year is 1940). Check both before citing.

Sound as counterpoint, from the early and modern theorists: non-synchronous sound and contrapuntal clash (Pudovkin's Deserter, the car-door example in The Broadway Melody) carry meaning that matching sound to image cannot. His Girl Friday shows dialogue, overlap and cutting working together. Good for the course's sound and edit section.

Hollywood's invisible editing as Fabe describes it: match cuts, motivated cuts and dissolves hide the edit, with the omniscient camera that knows more than the characters. Her His Girl Friday example times story against screen time (about 22 minutes of story in 11.5 minutes of screen time, by clock shots). Good for the course's continuity and story-time section.

Deep focus in Citizen Kane (Welles and Toland) as Fabe explains it: a foreground face, a middle-ground father and a far-off boy in one long take let the viewer choose where to look, as on a stage. Blocking and depth do the work that a cut would do elsewhere. Good for the course's lens section, paired with its note on depth of field.
Fabe says the mother-and-Thatcher scene is a single shot of over two minutes, and that Chaplin's longest shot was 47 seconds. Check the running time on a copy before quoting a length.

Transitions in Kane as Fabe lists them: dissolves that carry symbolic weight (the sled under snow), and the 'lightning mix', where sound continuity (an unfinished line of dialogue) joins shots years apart. Sound perspective: volume set so distant voices sound further away. Useful for the course's transitions and sound-perspective notes.

Neorealist production as Fabe describes it: location shooting, post-synchronised sound, nonprofessional actors, mobile camera and grainy stock to get a documentary look. Open City itself used studio interiors and expressionist lighting, so the look was a choice, not a rule. Useful for the course's low-budget and location sections.
The Figure 28 caption dates Open City to 1947; the film was released in 1945. Use 1945.

Shot-by-shot in The Bicycle Thief: a 3-4 second cut pattern (POV, reaction, match on movement) switches to an 18-second take that follows Ricci towards the bicycle with the camera, so the bicycle is small in deep focus and the decision happens in real space. Bazin's point: a long take keeps the real distance between objects; editing only implies it. Strong example for the course's coverage vs long-take choice.

A jump cut between shots 11 and 12 is used to show Ricci's moral reversal. Cutting off the action for a beat shows a change of mind through edit, not performance. Use as an example of a deliberate jump cut with a motivated reason.

Lens and framing as meaning in The 400 Blows: wide-angle deep-focus long shots with a moving camera for freedom; tight frames and grid shapes in the cell for confinement (the face framed as a noose). Shows a lens choice carrying emotion, which the course's lens module can cite.
The book calls the zoetrope an eighteenth-century toy. The zoetrope dates from the 1830s (the phenakistiscope about 1832). Correct before citing.

Long takes and freeze-frame in The 400 Blows: a 45-second take keeps the guard's distance from Antoine; a 75-second run tests real time; the closing freeze-frame breaks the illusion on purpose. Fabe also notes that the psychiatrist's questions were recorded later and dubbed. Useful as examples of deliberate self-reflexive technique.

Hitchcock's 'pure cinema' as the book sets it out, in the key-stealing sequence in Notorious: twelve shots, four establishing, the rest close-ups of hands, face and key; five are point-of-view shots that pull the viewer into Alicia's view; a tracking shot toward the key with rising music. Hitchcock's own rule: break the action into details so each one forces its meaning on the audience. Strong case for the course's coverage and POV sections.
Hitchcock's MacGuffin as he described it to Truffaut: the uranium 'didn't really matter; we were telling a love story'. Use the term with that caveat and not as a rule that plot objects never matter.

Deliberate continuity breaks as a meaning device: Fellini's mismatched backgrounds (priests moving between shots) and a movement match that jumps location make memory look unreliable. Reisz's rule that backgrounds must match is the baseline being broken. Use as a controlled example of when to break continuity, not as a licence.
Fabe's point on diegetic and nondiegetic sound: Rota's score is blurred into the diegetic world (boys clap on the beat, a singer repeats the theme). Use as an example for the sound section.

Style as statement, from Fabe on Allen: documentary or cinema verite look used for fiction (Husbands and Wives) and classical continuity for the 'fiction' scenes against jittery cuts for the 'real' ones (Deconstructing Harry). Shows that a camera style carries a claim about truth. Relevant to the course's choice of documentary vs staged style.

Lens distortion for menace as the book describes it in Do the Right Thing: Radio Raheem's face shot in a big close-up with a 10mm wide-angle lens, from low, Dutch angles, so his size and threat grow. The same film sets warm reds and carbon-arc light in a shot-to-shot clash. Useful for the lens and angle sections; the book credits cinematographer Ernest Dickerson.

Colour and light as metaphor in Do the Right Thing: the set was repainted and lit with carbon arcs to feel hot; red and blue filters clash within and between shots. The film's cinematographer said the location's 'molecules' were the reason not to use a back lot. Use as a note on location and colour, not as a rule.

Point of view as a choice of who looks: Fabe's reading of Mulvey (male gaze, fetish close-ups) and Rozema's reversal (the heroine as voyeur, the camera caressing a woman from her point of view). Useful for the POV and close-up sections as a reminder that POV assigns a viewer. Keep the mention to one line; the argument is contested.

Digital capture changes what a take can be: Fabe notes a film magazine holds about ten minutes, while digital can record far longer, so Figgis shot Timecode in one unbroken 93-minute take with four synchronised cameras, reshooting in one day. Cheap tape also let the cast risk improvisation. Relevant to the DSLR module's note that file and card limits shape the shoot.

The book's claim that digital pictures 'can be superior' (Manovich) and that viewers will soon be unable to tell digital from 35mm is a 2000 view. Treat both as dated; check current evidence before repeating.

The glossary gives usable shot vocabulary: movement, direction and eyeline match, the 180-degree line, shot/reverse shot, POV, cross-cut, contrast cut, and sound terms (diegetic, nondiegetic, internal-diegetic, metadiegetic, parallel, counterpoint). Good for the course's terminology list. Definitions are paraphrase-ready; quote no more than 15 words.
